articles.title: Governo Lula diz estar indignado com nova proposta de tarifa dos EUA contra o Brasil e que não 'cederá a esse tipo de ameaça' | G1
articles.standfirst: O governo americamo propôs nesta quarta (25) a cobrança de uma tarifa adicional de 10% sobre aeronaves brasileiras e o aumento da tributação sobre o açúcar importado do país.
articles.summary: O governo americamo propôs nesta quarta (25) a cobrança de uma tarifa adicional de 10% sobre aeronaves brasileiras e o aumento da tributação sobre o açúcar importado do país.
articles.body:
O governo brasileiro divulgou uma nota nesta quarta-feira (25) na qual manifestou "indignação" com a proposta do Escritório do Representante Comercial dos EUA (USTR, na sigla em inglês) para que sejam impostas novas tarifas sobre aeronaves brasileiras e o açúcar brasileiro (veja mais abaixo).

Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

"O governo brasileiro expressa indignação com a decisão do Escritório do Representante de Comércio dos Estados Unidos de recomendar a imposição de novas tarifas para a importação de aeronaves e açúcar", diz a nota.

Conforme a nota do Palácio do Planalto, o governo brasileiro vem negociando "de boa-fé" há mais de um ano com os americanos em relação à chamada Seção 301, acrescentando que os Estados Unidos ficaram de enviar uma proposta, o que não aconteceu antes da recomendação de tarifa.

"Fica evidente que a nova recomendação é feita como o objetivo de pressionar o governo para que haja alterações em medidas regulatórias nacionais relacionadas ao sistema de pagamentos PIX, comércio digital, acordos preferenciais, dentre outros, como consta do anúncio de hoje. A decisão unilateral do USTR constitui uma ação inaceitável dentro do processo negociador bilateral em curso. O Brasil não cederá a esse tipo de ameaça", acrescentou o governo.

Com base na Seção 301, a Casa Branca decidiu impor dois tarifaços sobre produtos brasileiros vendidos no mercado americano:

um de 25%: em razão do entendimento de que o Brasil adota práticas desleais na economia em relação a empresários americanos em áreas como PIX, etanol, propriedade intelectual e desmatamento;

outro de 12,5%: em razão do entendimento de que dezenas de países, incluindo o Brasil, falharam ao coibir a importação de mercadorias produzidas em locais onde há trabalho forçado.

Conforme a nota divulgada pelo governo brasileiro nesta quarta-feira, a decisão do USTR "constitui uma ação inaceitável dentro do processo negociador bilateral em curso. O Brasil não cederá a esse tipo de ameaça".

"O Brasil seguirá buscando uma saída negociada, sem prejuízo de ações no âmbito da OMC e sem descartar a possibilidade de adoção de medidas de reciprocidade frente à aplicação ilegal e injusta de tarifas contra produtos brasileiros", completou.

A proposta que afeta o país foi anunciada pelo representante comercial americano, Jamieson Greer, e altera medidas definidas após uma investigação do USTR, que confirmou a aplicação de uma tarifa adicional de 25% sobre produtos brasileiros em julho.

Na ocasião, os Estados Unidos criaram uma lista de exceções para produtos considerados estratégicos. Entre os itens isentos estavam aeronaves prontas e determinadas exportações brasileiras de açúcar acima das cotas estabelecidas.

Com as mudanças propostas, aeronaves brasileiras prontas passariam a pagar uma tarifa de 10% para entrar no mercado americano. A mudança pode afetar especialmente a Embraer, fabricante brasileira de aeronaves.

Segundo Greer, o Brasil não respondeu às reclamações apresentadas nas negociações realizadas ao longo de mais de um ano. Por isso, o governo americano propôs novas tarifas para pressionar o país a mudar práticas comerciais que considera prejudiciais à sua economia.

Sem acordo com Brasil, EUA impuseram tarifas de 25% contra alguns produtos — Foto: Joao Oliveira/Zoonar/picture alliance

Em julho desse ano, o governo brasileiro acionou a Organização Mundial do Comércio (OMC) contra o tarifaço imposto por Donald Trump sobre produtos brasileiros exportados para os Estados Unidos, formalizando o chamado "pedido de consulta".

🔎 O pedido de consulta é a primeira etapa de uma disputa na OMC e abre espaço para que os países tentem chegar a um acordo antes de um julgamento.

Na prática, a partir do início das consultas, os países têm 60 dias para tentar chegar a um acordo. Ao final desse prazo, sem acordo, qualquer um dos dois países poderia pedir a abertura de um painel.

O bloqueio, no entanto, não encerra a disputa. O Brasil poderá reapresentar o pedido em uma próxima reunião da OMC. Na segunda tentativa, os EUA não poderão impedir sozinhos a criação do painel: para barrá-la, todos os membros da organização terão de concordar.

Nota à imprensa sobre as tarifas dos Estados Unidos para aeronaves e açúcar brasileiro

O governo brasileiro expressa indignação sobre a decisão do Escritório de Representação de Comércio dos Estados Unidos de recomendar a imposição de novas tarifas para a importação de aeronaves e açúcar.

Há mais de um ano estamos atuando de boa-fé em negociações relativas à Seção 301 da Lei de Comércio de 1974.

No dia 21 de agosto, os presidentes Lula e Donald Trump se falaram por telefone e acertaram constituir um grupo de trabalho entre os dois países sobre temas comerciais.

Em 31 de agosto, os ministros Mauro Vieira, das Relações Exteriores (MRE), e Márcio Elias Rosa, do Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços (MDIC), realizaram reunião virtual com o Representante de Comércio dos Estados Unidos (USTR), Jamieson Greer. Na ocasião, o USTR se comprometeu a enviar os termos de referência de um possível acordo econômico e comercial entre os dois países.

No dia 30 de setembro, houve nova reunião presencial entre os ministros Mauro Vieira e Márcio Elias Rosa com Greer.

Até hoje os referidos termos de referência não foram enviados, apesar das repetidas cobranças feitas pelo governo brasileiro.

Fica evidente que a nova recomendação é feita como o objetivo de pressionar o governo para que haja alterações em medidas regulatórias nacionais relacionadas ao sistema de pagamentos PIX, comércio digital, acordos preferenciais, dentre outros, com consta do anuncio de hoje.

A decisão unilateral do USTR constitui uma ação inaceitável dentro do processo negociador bilateral em curso. O Brasil não cederá a esse tipo de ameaça.

O Brasil seguirá buscando uma saída negociada, sem prejuízo de ações no âmbito da OMC e sem descartar a possibilidade de adoção de medidas de reciprocidade frente à aplicação ilegal e injusta de tarifas contra produtos brasileiros.

articles.title: Dólar cai a R$ 5,81, com novas tarifas de Trump e medidas econômicas de Lula no radar; Ibovespa sobe | G1
articles.standfirst: A moeda americana caiu 1,58%, cotada a R$ 5,8167. Já o principal índice da bolsa brasileira subiu 1,58%, aos 166.675 pontos.
articles.summary: A moeda americana caiu 1,58%, cotada a R$ 5,8167. Já o principal índice da bolsa brasileira subiu 1,58%, aos 166.675 pontos.
articles.body:
Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

O dólar inverteu o sinal positivo visto na primeira hora do pregão e fechou em queda nesta quarta-feira (25). A moeda caiu 1,58% , cotada a R$ 5,8167 . Na máxima da sessão, chegou a R$ 5,9703 . Já o Ibovespa , principal índice da bolsa brasileira, subiu 1,58% , aos 166.675 pontos .

A nova rodada de tarifas anunciada pelo governo de Donald Trump sobre produtos de 14 parceiros comerciais, incluindo o Brasil, segue no radar dos investidores. Para o país, a proposta prevê uma tarifa adicional de 10% sobre aeronaves prontas e aumento da tributação sobre o açúcar, o que pode afetar a Embraer. As medidas ainda passarão por consulta pública e não estão em vigor. ( Veja mais abaixo )

▶️ Novas medidas econômicas preparadas pelo governo também estão no centro das atenções. Segundo o ministro do planejamento, Bruno Moretti, a ideia é que a nova PEC traga novas propostas de ajuste econômico, com o objetivo de dar mais "potência fiscal" e segurança de que o governo cumprirá a meta de resultado primário (diferença entre receitas e despesas). As informações são do blog da Ana Flor .

🔎 A notícia de que as iniciativas teriam foco no controle de despesas trouxe alívio para o real na véspera, fazendo com que a moeda brasileira tivesse um desempenho superior ao de seus pares. Veja mais.

▶️ O mercado também segue atento às medidas econômicas que o governo tenta aprovar antes do recesso parlamentar, que começa em 23 de dezembro. Entre os projetos para aprovação, estão duas medidas que determinarão o Orçamento de 2027 e a MP do Imposto Seletivo. Com isso, investidores seguem alertas sobre eventuais impactos no cenário fiscal.

▶️ Na agenda econômica, o destaque fica com os novos dados de inflação e atividade dos EUA. O PCE, índice de despesas de consumo pessoal e medida de preços preferida do Federal Reserve ( Fed , o banco central dos EUA), subiu 0,3% em outubro, em linha com o esperado pelo mercado. Já o PIB americano cresceu a uma taxa anualizada de 4,3% no terceiro trimestre. (veja mais abaixo)

🔎 Outros indicadores, como o Livro Bege e os pedidos iniciais de seguro-desemprego também serão acompanhados.

Veja abaixo mais detalhes sobre o dia nos mercados.

O governo de Donald Trump propôs nesta quarta-feira uma nova rodada de tarifas de importação sobre produtos de 14 parceiros comerciais dos EUA, incluindo Brasil, China, União Europeia, Japão e Índia . As taxas ainda não estão em vigor e variam de 15% a 35% , conforme o país ou bloco.

No caso do Brasil, a proposta prevê uma tarifa adicional de 10% sobre aeronaves prontas e o aumento da tributação sobre o açúcar exportado aos americanos. A mudança pode afetar especialmente a Embraer, fabricante brasileira de aeronaves.

As medidas alteram as exceções concedidas em julho, quando os EUA estabeleceram uma tarifa adicional de 25% sobre produtos brasileiros, mas pouparam alguns itens considerados estratégicos, entre eles aeronaves prontas e determinadas exportações de açúcar.

🔎 A nova rodada também prevê tarifas de até 35% para o Vietnã; até 25% para a Índia; até 20% para China e Singapura; até 18% para Bangladesh, Camboja, Indonésia, Malásia e Tailândia; e até 15% para União Europeia, Japão, Coreia do Sul, Suíça e Taiwan.

No caso da China, a alíquota geral proposta é de até 20%, mas algumas mercadorias terão tarifas menores, de até 10%, enquanto outras ficarão isentas. A proposta considera também o acordo firmado entre Trump e o presidente chinês, Xi Jinping , em outubro de 2025.

Segundo o governo americano, os países e blocos atingidos adotam políticas que estimulam a produção industrial acima da demanda, criando um excesso de oferta e prejudicando empresas e trabalhadores dos EUA. As propostas ainda passarão por consulta pública antes de entrar em vigor.

O ministro do Planejamento, Bruno Moretti, afirmou ao blog da Ana Flor , na última terça-feira (24) que o governo prepara o texto de uma Proposta de Emenda à Constituição (PEC) com mais medidas de ajuste econômico.

Segundo Moretti, a proposta, somada ao projeto de lei aprovado nesta madrugada na Câmara, trará mais “potência fiscal” e vai dar a segurança de que o governo cumprirá a meta de resultado primário.

Moretti reforça que o presidente Lula “autorizou e participa” da discussão das medidas, que devem acelerar o esforço de controlar a dívida pública – sem cortes em programas sociais ou em promessas de campanha.

Na avaliação do ministro, o projeto aprovado na Câmara é emergencial e também estrutural, não apenas servindo para o orçamento de 2027, mas também para os anos futuros.

➡️ A Câmara dos Deputados aprovou o projeto de lei que promove um ajuste nas contas públicas para viabilizar o cumprimento da meta fiscal de 2027 na última segunda-feira. A proposta, que segue para sanção do presidente Lula (PT), reúne medidas que podem gerar uma economia de até R$ 56 bilhões já no próximo ano.

Além disso, o governo também corre contra o tempo para aprovar uma série de medidas econômicas até o recesso parlamentar, que começa em 23 de dezembro. Em menos de um mês, governistas tentam acelerar a análise de ao menos oito projetos.

PEC do IPI (Imposto Sobre Produtos Industrializados);

Lei de Diretrizes Orçamentárias (LDO) de 2027;

Definição da alíquota do CBS (imposto sobre consumo da reforma tributária);

O índice de preços PCE, principal medida de inflação acompanhada pelo Federal Reserve (Fed, o banco central americano), subiu 0,3% em outubro, em linha com o esperado pelo mercado. Em 12 meses, o indicador acumula alta de 3,8%.

O resultado reforça a expectativa de que o Fed volte a elevar os juros em dezembro e faça um novo aumento no início de 2027.

A economia dos EUA cresceu a uma taxa anualizada de 4,3% no terceiro trimestre, acima dos 3,4% calculados inicialmente e da expectativa de 3,5% do mercado. Esse foi o ritmo mais acelerado em três anos, segundo o Escritório de Análise Econômica (BEA, na sigla em inglês), ligado ao Departamento de Comércio americano.

A revisão para cima refletiu, principalmente, estimativas maiores para os gastos dos consumidores e os investimentos das empresas, sobretudo os relacionados à inteligência artificial.

O número de americanos que entraram com novos pedidos de auxílio-desemprego caiu mais do que o esperado na semana passada, indicando que as demissões permanecem em níveis baixos.

Os pedidos iniciais de auxílio-desemprego caíram em 13 mil, para 189 mil, em dado com ajuste sazonal, na semana encerrada em 21 de novembro, informou o Departamento do Trabalho nesta quarta-feira.

Economistas consultados pela Reuters esperavam 200 mil pedidos. O relatório foi publicado um dia antes do previsto devido ao feriado de Ação de Graças, celebrado nesta quinta-feira nos EUA.

Os pedidos permanecem em níveis historicamente baixos. Apesar do ritmo mais fraco de contratações, as demissões também seguem reduzidas, quadro que economistas têm descrito como de “baixa contratação e baixa demissão”.

Os principais índices de Wall Street fecharam sem direção única nesta quarta-feira (25), após uma onda de vendas de ações de tecnologia provocar perdas mais acentuadas ao longo do pregão. No fechamento, porém, investidores aproveitaram os preços mais baixos para comprar ações, reduzindo as perdas antes do feriado de Ação de Graças nos EUA.

O Dow Jones subiu 0,31%, aos 50.173,90 pontos. Já o S&P 500 recuou 0,25%, aos 7.183,08 pontos, e o Nasdaq , que reúne principalmente empresas de tecnologia, caiu 0,65%, aos 23.579,44 pontos.

Os principais índices europeus também fecharam em queda. O STOXX 600 , que reúne empresas de diferentes países da região, recuou 1%, aos 626,03 pontos.

Entre as principais bolsas da região, o DAX , da Alemanha, caiu 1,26%; o CAC 40 , da França, perdeu 0,75%; e o FTSE 100 , do Reino Unido, recuou 0,38%.

Na Ásia , as bolsas também fecharam em queda generalizada. Os investidores repercutiram o desempenho negativo de Wall Street na véspera, quando as ações de tecnologia estiveram entre as principais responsáveis pelas perdas.

O SSEC , da bolsa de Xangai, caiu 2,03%, enquanto o CSI 300 , que reúne as principais empresas listadas em Xangai e Shenzhen, recuou 1,65%. Na Coreia do Sul, o Kospi perdeu 6,16%. O Hang Seng , de Hong Kong, caiu 1,14%, e o Nikkei, do Japão, recuou 2,78%.

* Com informações das agências de notícias Reuters e France Presse.

articles.title: Home Depot and Lowe's sent U.S. jobs to India before Kroger
articles.summary: The savings are huge, but many of the people who shop there won’t like it when they find out how.
articles.body:
Lowe's only operates stores in the United States, but the chain has sent thousands of jobs to India.

Rival Home Depot has a broader footprint with stores in Mexico and Canada, along with its U.S. base, but it's not a global company, and it too has moved white-collar American jobs to an operations center in India.

Both companies brag about the audience they serve on their websites.

"Our team proudly serves approximately 16 million customer transactions per week in the United States. Lowe's operates over 1,700 home improvement stores and employs approximately 300,000 associates," Lowe's shared.

"Today, The Home Depot is the world's largest home improvement retailer with approximately 475,000 orange-blooded associates and more than 2,300 stores in the U.S., Canada and Mexico," it posted .

Neither company's website mentions prominently that the chains have shipped thousands of jobs from the U.S. to India, a country where neither home improvement giant operates even a single store.

While Lowe's has not mentioned its India office in any of its recent earnings calls, it does have a LinkedIn page that describes just how big its commitment outside the U.S. has grown.

"Lowe's India, the Global Capability Center of Lowe's Companies Inc., is a hub for driving the Fortune 100 retailer's technology, business, analytics, and shared services strategy. Based in Bengaluru with over 4,500 associates, it powers innovations across omnichannel retail, AI/ML, enterprise architecture, supply chain, and customer experience," the company shared.

The company's growth in India comes at a time when it has cut U.S. jobs as part of its "perpetual productivity improvement" (PPI) plan, an effort to save $1 billion annually.

"This commitment to PPI is at the center of the announcement we made recently to eliminate approximately 600 corporate and support roles. Although these are difficult decisions to make, this workforce reduction will help us create greater financial agility within our dynamic industry while continuing to invest in customer-facing areas of the company," CEO Marvin Ellison said during his chain's fourth-quarter earnings call .

Lowe's celebrated an expansion of its India office in October.

"The ceremony included the unveiling of the new workspace, a traditional lamp-lighting ceremony, and the signing of the gable. The leadership team also took part in an office walkthrough, giving employees an opportunity to experience the new facility," GCC Pulse reported.

articles.title: Why India is betting Rs 11,000 crore on construction, infrastructure equipment manufacturing - explained
articles.summary: The Union Cabinet has approved an Rs 11,000-crore scheme to strengthen India's construction and infrastructure equipment (CIE) manufacturing ecosystem,
articles.body: The Union Cabinet has approved an Rs 11,000-crore scheme to strengthen India's construction and infrastructure equipment (CIE) manufacturing ecosystem, with a focus on increasing domestic production, supporting component makers and setting up a dedicated testing facility.The decisions were announced by Union minister Ashwini Vaishnaw at a press briefing following the Cabinet meeting chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi.The Scheme for Enhancement of Construction and Infrastructure Equipment Manufacturing Ecosystem will be implemented by the Ministry of Heavy Industries over eight years, starting from the 2026-27 financial year.It is intended to incentivise manufacturers to expand production of technologically advanced equipment and reduce dependence on external supply chains.The government has identified equipment such as ship-to-shore cranes, tunnel boring machines, hydraulic excavators and off-highway trucks as areas the scheme aims to support.The approval comes as the government is also clearing major infrastructure projects, including a second container terminal at Kamarajar Port in Tamil Nadu and a greenfield airport at Doloo in Assam.The port project has been approved at an estimated cost of Rs 4,288.26 crore, while the airport project has an outlay of Rs 2,014 crore.Why has the government introduced the scheme?India's construction and infrastructure equipment industry is currently the world's third largest, behind China and the United States. Its market size stood at around Rs 97,500 crore in 2024-25, according to the ministry of heavy industries.The sector is expected to expand significantly as investment in infrastructure, including roads and ports, and housing increases. The government projects that the domestic market will more than double to around Rs 2.28 lakh crore by 2029-30.Construction and infrastructure projects require a range of specialised equipment, from machinery used in excavation and tunnelling to cranes deployed at ports and equipment used in large-scale industrial and road construction.The scheme seeks to encourage domestic manufacturers to produce more of this equipment and its components. It also aims to strengthen India's position in the global CIE market by developing indigenous manufacturing capabilities and improving supply chain security.The government has linked the initiative to the Atmanirbhar Bharat programme and its broader objective of building a self-reliant industrial base.How will the Rs 11,000-crore scheme work?The scheme has two main components: a sales-linked incentive programme for manufacturers and financial support for setting up a dedicated testing facility.1. Sales-linked incentives for manufacturersThe first component will provide incentives based on the incremental sales value of eligible construction and infrastructure equipment and components.The benefits will be available to approved applicants in two categories:Original equipment manufacturers (OEMs)Component manufacturersThe incentive rates will be graded, ranging from 13% to 8% of incremental sales value over a five-year period.This component is intended to encourage manufacturers to expand domestic production and increase sales of eligible equipment and components.2. Grant for a dedicated testing facilityThe second component provides a grant of up to Rs 375 crore, in the form of viability gap funding, for establishing a dedicated CIE testing facility in India.The facility is intended to support testing of construction and infrastructure equipment within the country. The provision forms part of the government's effort to develop the domestic ecosystem alongside manufacturing capacity.What is the implementation timeline?The scheme will run for eight years, from 2026-27 to 2033-34, with implementation divided into three stages.PeriodWhat happensFY2026-27 to FY2027-28Two-year gestation period for setting up manufacturing facilitiesFY2028-29 to FY2032-33Five-year period for disbursing incentivesFY2033-34Settlement of incentives linked to incremental sales in FY2032-33The initial two years will allow approved applicants to establish manufacturing facilities. Incentives will then be disbursed over the following five years, based on incremental sales of eligible equipment and components. The final year will be used to settle incentives for the last year of the disbursement period.Which equipment will benefit?The scheme is aimed at technologically advanced construction and infrastructure equipment used across major infrastructure and industrial projects.The government has specifically identified:Ship-to-shore cranes: Equipment used to load and unload containers between ships and port terminals.Tunnel boring machines: Specialised machinery used to excavate tunnels for infrastructure projects.Hydraulic excavators: Machines used for digging, earthmoving and other construction activities.Off-highway trucks: Heavy-duty vehicles used to transport materials at construction, mining and industrial sites.The scheme also covers eligible components manufactured by approved applicants, rather than focusing only on finished equipment.What does the government expect from the scheme?The government expects the incentives to expand domestic manufacturing capacity, improve the availability of equipment and components, strengthen supply chains and create employment opportunities.The proposed testing facility is another part of the effort to develop the domestic manufacturing ecosystem.With the CIE market projected to grow from around Rs 97,500 crore in 2024-25 to Rs 2.28 lakh crore by 2029-30, the scheme is intended to support manufacturers as demand for construction and infrastructure equipment rises.The government has positioned the initiative as part of its Atmanirbhar Bharat agenda, with the stated objective of making India more self-reliant in technologically advanced equipment manufacturing and more competitive in global markets.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: Montse Cespedosa, experta en hipotecas, explica los dos miedos existentes a la hora de comprar una vivienda: “El FOMO y el FOOP”
articles.standfirst: Estos temores pueden condicionar una compra
articles.summary: Estos temores pueden condicionar una compra
articles.body: Uno de los objetivos de las personas es poder acceder a una hipoteca y comprarse una vivienda que, con el paso de los años, se convierta en el hogar de la familia. Sin embargo, ahora la sociedad observa un momento complicado en cuanto a la adquisición de viviendas en ciertos lugares, sobre todo por el encarecimiento y la falta de oferta. Además, las condiciones de los tipos de interés ofrecidos por las entidades bancarias ya no son tan rentables como hace meses atrás, por lo que la elección de todo lo que engloba un inmueble se puede convertir en trascendental, y una mala decisión puede encarecer sobremanera el coste de la propiedad. Precisamente hay dos miedos que se han instaurado en cuanto a la compra de viviendas se refiere y los explica la experta en hipotecas Montse Cespedosa en un vídeo compartido en sus redes sociales. Estos miedos están instaurados en otros sectores de la sociedad y son el ‘FOMO’ y el ‘FOOP’. “Hasta ahora dominaba el FOMO, el ‘Fear of Missing Out’, es el miedo a quedarte fuera, el comprar corriendo antes de que te lo quiten. Compras una vivienda y firmas una hipoteca casi sin mirar lo que estás haciendo por el miedo a perder esa operación”, explica Cespedosa antes de introducir un segundo término menos conocido. “Este 2027 habrá un nuevo miedo y será el FOOP, el ‘Fear of Overpaying’. Es cuando el mercado se frena y tú te paralizas por miedo a pagar de más de lo que valdrá mañana”, explica. “Lees titulares de que las ventas caen y piensas: ‘¿y si compro ahora y el año que viene vale menos?’. Entonces esperas, y esperas, y sigues esperando…”, sentencia. Para finalizar, explica una de las paradojas que incluyen estos dos miedos: “Con FOMO compras cuando peor puedes negociar. Con FOOP te paralizas justo cuando más podrías negociar”.

articles.summary: President Donald Trump is preparing to impose a new round of tariffs on China and dozens of other countries, seeking to revive his trade agenda after the Supreme Court struck down the sweeping global tariffs he introduced earlier this year.
articles.body: President Donald Trump is preparing to impose a new round of tariffs on China and dozens of other countries, seeking to revive his trade agenda after the Supreme Court struck down the sweeping global tariffs he introduced earlier this year. China and Vietnam are set to face a 20% tariff, the highest proposed rate among the 14 trading partners targeted by the investigation. Rates could go even higher if countries don’t adhere to pre-existing trade agreements. For China, it could rise to 40%, and for Vietnam, 35%. Meanwhile, the European Union’s proposed starting rate would be 15%, but it could go up to 20%. The earliest the administration expects the tariffs to take effect is January, the official said. Before imposing the tariffs, the administration must complete a public notice-and-comment process and hold hearings, the official said. The proposal calls for broad exclusions for energy, food that can’t easily be grown in the US, certain semiconductor chips and pharmaceuticals. Additionally, they would not stack with existing duties on products such as automobiles, steel and aluminum. Americans are unlikely to see prices rise substantially from the tariff changes, in part because of the exclusions, but also since businesses have already factored these rates, which mirror prior levels, into pricing. These latest tariffs stem from a monthslong investigation undertaken by the Office of the US Trade Representative into whether foreign governments are incentivizing excess manufacturing through measures like subsidies, and favorable loan terms. The administration argues this allows foreign companies to produce more than they otherwise would and then sell at artificially low prices, undercutting their American competitors. The White House official said he believes retaliation will be limited and noted that trading partners received advanced notice of the proposed actions. The announcement comes after Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping struck a notably friendly tone during their recent meeting. Trump, meanwhile, took credit for getting Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO on Monday, despite bipartisan concerns around whether China is using advanced Nvidia chips to bolster its military capabilities by bypassing export restrictions. Post-election maneuver With the bruising midterm elections behind them, Trump officials appear keen on turning their attention back to the president’s trade agenda. That’s unlikely to score well with voters and some Republican lawmakers. Two-thirds of voters said Trump’s tariffs hurt the national economy, according to nationwide results of CNN’s Voter Poll. Nearly the same share said they hurt the local economy, too. Voters took their frustration with Trump’s tariffs to the polls in the midterms, electing an unprecedented number of Democrats, many of whom hail from historically Republican states and districts. Since the election, a growing number of Republicans, including Sens. Ted Cruz and Todd Young, have publicly raised concerns about Trump’s tariff policies. Their opposition could present a growing obstacle to the president’s trade agenda if they join Democrats in challenging it. “One of the causes of increased costs is that our current tariff structure is overly broad, and as a result, it is negatively affecting too many American factory floors, farms, small businesses, and family budgets,” Young said in a post on X after the midterm elections. “I’ve said for over a year that our tariff policy must be tied to clear objectives focused on protecting America’s economic and national security.”

articles.title: US announces new tariffs of up to 20% on China, the EU, and 12 other nations
articles.summary: The duties could be a shock to the global economy, with China a main target.
articles.body:
The Trump administration on Wednesday proposed new tariffs of up to 20% on China, the European Union, and 12 other major US trading partners to take effect next year, following an eight-month investigation into excess manufacturing capacity.

The duties could be a shock to the global economy, with China a main target.

The proposed 20% tariff on many Chinese goods was described by the Trump administration as a "deal rate" that could go higher depending on how ongoing talks progress. The new tariff would be stacked on top of at least some preexisting tariffs, resulting in a total rate of over 40% on some goods.

The new tariffs won't go into effect until after additional hearings and a public comment period and "probably will be in January at the earliest," according to a US official who briefed reporters ahead of the announcement.

An existing trade truce with China is set to expire on Jan. 10.

Several other Asian nations are also in line for higher duties, with a new 20% tariff proposed for Vietnam. Cambodia, Indonesia, and Malaysia are in line for 18% rates. India would have a 17% rate, but only, the administration said, if ongoing talks produce a deal.

The new rate announcements were accompanied by detailed investigative reports on each country, with China's report alone spanning 456 pages.

China immediately pushed back, with a Foreign Ministry spokesperson saying "the so-called issue of overcapacity is a false proposition, and China opposes using it as a pretext for political manipulation," according to state media .

The US official said the rates could go even higher depending on how the countries respond, and added that the investigation had concluded that a new 40% tariff on China and a 35% rate on Vietnam was "warranted," even as a lower rate is being proposed for now due to ongoing talks.

On Wednesday, the White House listed an array of "Proposed Rates" that were higher across the board, ranging from 20% to 40%, and announced plans to modify some tariffs on Brazil with an additional 10% tariff on sugar and finished aircraft.

The effects elsewhere could be more muted, with new duties designed not to overstep rates negotiated in recent trade deals. That meant trading partners, including the EU, South Korea, and Japan, would all see a 15% tariff rate, which is in line with what they negotiated in recent months.

"We're sticking to that," when it comes to these nations, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a CNBC appearance Wednesday, "because we think a lot of these deals we made actually solve a lot of problems we see in excess capacity."

articles.body: The Donald Trump administration on Wednesday proposed fresh tariffs on 14 of Washington's major trading partners, including India, citing concerns over "excess industrial capacity" and its adverse impact on US commerce, Reuters reported.The proposed measures follow an eight-month investigation conducted by the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) under Section 301, which examined alleged unfair trade practices involving 16 trading partners.The countries and trading blocs targeted by the proposed tariffs include China, Bangladesh, Cambodia, the European Union, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.However, Mexico and Norway have been left out of the proposed measures for now.A senior US official told Reuters that Washington had determined that these countries "create, sustain, or contribute to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors" through policies and practices considered "unreasonable' and "harmful" to US commerce.India and Vietnam, in particular, are among the countries that have yet to conclude trade agreements with the US.China is expected to face the highest cumulative tariff burden. The proposed 20% duties would come in addition to tariffs of around 25% imposed during Trump's first presidential term.However, the new duties would not be levied over the 10% or 12.5% tariffs introduced in July over allegations that certain countries had failed to adequately enforce anti-forced labour laws.Beijing, however, has rejected the allegations, arguing that its exports are driven by the country's competitive advantages, Reuters reported.Meanwhile, the US official also said the proposed measures would adhere to tariff limits established under existing trade agreements. articles.title: Flipkart CEO Kalyan Krishnamurthy in sudden exit after decade at helm
articles.summary: Flipkart CEO Kalyan Krishnamurthy to exit on Dec 4 after nearly a decade, amid reported differences with Walmart over IPO timing and profitability goals.
articles.body: Bengaluru: In an abrupt leadership transition at one of India’s most valuable internet companies, Flipkart group CEO Kalyan Krishnamurthy is leaving the Walmart-owned e-commerce major after nearly a decade at the helm, amid differences with its US parent over the company’s public listing plans and financial priorities.Krishnamurthy’s last working day will be Dec 4, barely nine days after the announcement, according to an internal communication from Walmart International president and CEO Chris Nicholas to Flipkart employees, reviewed by TOI. An emergency town hall was called on Wednesday as news of his departure caught even sections of the company’s senior leadership off guard.“Most of us were largely left clueless that the CEO is about to exit like this. So sudden. It’s not like any tension building up between the leadership looked apparent to employees,” a senior Flipkart executive told TOI on condition of anonymity.Flipkart has not named a permanent successor. Chief product and technology officer Balaji Thiagarajan, along with the Flipkart board, will lead the company in the interim. A new CEO will be announced in the coming weeks.Neither the internal communication nor the company’s public announcement specified the reasons for Krishnamurthy’s departure or whether it was his decision to leave.The exit comes against the backdrop of differences between Flipkart’s leadership and Walmart over the timing of its much-awaited initial public offering (IPO). The Economic Times reported that Krishnamurthy met Walmart’s leadership in Bentonville, US, earlier this month, where disagreements emerged over the listing plans and a liquidity event for the company’s leadership and employees.Flipkart had completed the process of shifting its domicile from Singapore to India in March this year, a crucial step towards a domestic listing. However, plans for an IPO were subsequently put on hold following Walmart president and CEO John Furner’s visit to Bengaluru in May. The US retail giant has reportedly sought operating break-even at the Ebitda level by the end of FY27 before considering a public listing or fresh external fundraising.The delay has also become a source of discontent among current and former employees holding stock options. In October, a group of former senior executives wrote to Walmart’s board seeking a buyout of their vested stock options. Flipkart has also witnessed a series of senior-level departures this year, including that of longstanding group chief financial officer Sriram Venkataraman.Krishnamurthy’s successor will have to balance Walmart’s profitability expectations with the need to invest aggressively in an increasingly competitive market. Besides its longstanding rivalry with Amazon, Flipkart faces competition from Meesho in affordable online retail and Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart in quick commerce.Flipkart’s consolidated net loss narrowed marginally to Rs 8,468 crore in FY26 from Rs 8,646 crore a year earlier, even as operating revenue grew 18% to Rs 1.46 lakh crore.Krishnamurthy, a former Tiger Global executive, returned to Flipkart in 2016 when the company was struggling to fend off Amazon. He was elevated to CEO in January 2017 and subsequently oversaw Walmart’s $16 billion acquisition of a majority stake in the company in 2018 and its transition from a founder-led business.Under Krishnamurthy, Flipkart’s business grew more than fivefold, the company said.“I am proud of the scale of the business we have built, but equally proud of how we have built it. Strong ethics, integrity and high standards of governance have been central to Flipkart’s growth,” Krishnamurthy said in a statement.Money habits form by age 7. Is your child learning the right ones? articles.title: US economy grew faster last quarter than initially reported
articles.summary: The US economy boomed last quarter, growing at an annualized rate of 4.3%, the Commerce Department reported on Wednesday. That’s a massive jump from the 3.4% rate initially reported. Both figures take inflation into account.
articles.body: The US economy boomed last quarter, growing at an annualized rate of 4.3%, the Commerce Department reported on Wednesday. That’s a massive jump from the 3.4% rate initially reported. Both figures take inflation into account. Business investment, boosted by software spending, was the single biggest driver of the third-quarter surge, a sign of major AI-related spending. Consumer spending, which accounts for three quarters of gross domestic product, also played a key role in delivering the best quarter of economic growth in three years. But that robust growth comes with an inflation complication. In separate data released Wednesday, the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index — the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge — showed prices accelerated slightly to an annualized rate of 3.8% in October from 3.7% the prior month. That’s almost double the Fed’s target of 2%, solidifying the case for a rate hike next month. On a monthly basis, price increases slowed to 0.3% from 0.5% in September. The booming economy isn’t translating into increased wealth for many Americans, whose savings have dwindled as income growth has slowed. While Wednesday’s PCE report showed that the personal savings rate (savings as a percentage of after-tax income) rose 0.5 percentage points to 4.1%, it’s below the 4.9% rate seen in October of last year. The increase in savings came from a boost in after-tax income growth last month, though much of that was tied to Medicare rebate payments. But in a potentially worrisome sign for the economy, Americans are reining in their spending: When stripping out the 0.3% monthly price increase, spending was flat for October. “The cautious consumer is back. It will be a bargain-hunting holiday for many Americans,” Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, wrote in a note Wednesday.

LeBron James is one of the richest athletes in the world. But if you ask him, he'd tell you he's barely getting by.

During a Sept. 18, 2025 interview on Complex's (1) "360 With Speedy," host Speedy Morman asked about the basketball legend's reported $1.2 billion fortune at the time (1). James laughed and said, "Google search is a lie," then claimed the real figure is much lower.

"It's a couple, like, thousand in my bank," he said. "I ain't got nothing. I'm broke."

He said his watch, clothes and even his wedding band were all free, and that his kids now have "all the money."

It appears James was joking — or at least exaggerating.

Now in his 24th season, James is on track to have socked away (2) just over $585 million in career earnings on his NBA salary by the end of the 2026-2027 season, according to salary tracker Spotrac. That would be the most of any player in the league's history, according to Bleacher Report (3).

But that $585 million is only part of the story.

Forbes' net worth tracker pegs James' net worth at $1.4 billion (4), the only active NBA player worth $1 billion, largely due to his business deals (5). However, it's important to remember net worth doesn't necessarily equal spending money. Having your wealth tied up in a fleet of businesses can make it hard to access.

James, now 41 and playing for the Philadelphia 76ers, still takes his money seriously. On his wife Savannah James' podcast, "Everybody's Crazy," in October 2025, he said the first thing he told his financial advisor (6) was that if the advisor ever stole his money, or if James ended up broke, "it ain't going to be good for you."

Jokes aside, this money mindfulness touches on a real problem facing many pro athletes.

Plenty of pro athletes have earned fortunes, only to lose them after they stop playing.

Antoine Walker, a former Boston Celtics star and three-time NBA All-Star, is one example. He earned about $110 million in salary over 13 seasons, and more from endorsements, according to ESPN (7).

articles.title: Trump proposes a new wave of tariffs on China, E.U. and other trade partners
articles.summary: Trump proposes a new wave of tariffs on China, E.U. and other trade partners
articles.body: The Trump administration on Wednesday proposed a new wave of tariffs on the European Union, China and other trade partners, the result of a probe into what it says are unfair manufacturing practices. Some of the proposals include tariffs of at least 20% on China, which would match an agreement reached with the White House. But the duties could reach up to 40% if talks between the two countries fail. The United States’ current trade truce with China was recently extended and is set to expire in January. The tariffs will be implemented under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, a statute that the White House has relied upon more frequently for trade authority ever since the Supreme Court blocked many of Trump’s 2025 country-specific tariffs, imposed under a different authority. Wednesday’s announcement came less than a month after Trump’s tariff policies — and the inflation they fueled — contributed to Republicans’ sweeping losses in the midterm elections. Inflation hit 3.7% in September, driven primarily by energy prices, but also by higher prices of goods. In announcing the details of the new duties, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said that the overall rates applied to each trading partner would not surpass levels that were previously agreed to as part of bilateral framework trade deals. “When it all nets out, it really will just top up a few percentage points,” Greer said on CNBC. “So what we’re proposing today are actually a set of targeted tariffs to respond to this problem of excess capacity,” he added. For example, Trump agreed to cap tariffs on E.U. imports at 15% as part of a deal reached in 2025. On Wednesday, the trade representative reiterated that cap. The new tariffs will not stack on top of existing duties, except for the case of China. “We’ve talked to our trading partners about this,” Greer said. “They know what we’re proposing. I think a lot of this is baked in, and I don’t think any of these would actually take effect earlier than a couple of months from now.” He said he expects that “a broad” negotiation with trading partners would follow Wednesday’s proposals. But tensions continue to flare with trading partners, especially between Canada, the E.U. and China. Overnight, a spokesperson for the Chinese Commerce Ministry rejected the basis for the new tariffs. “Tariff wars and trade wars are in the interests of neither side,” the spokesperson said in a briefing for reporters. “So-called ‘overcapacity’ is a false proposition,” the spokesperson added. “China opposes using it as a pretext for political manipulation.” Separately, the European Union said its members “strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity. To the contrary, Europe is among those most exposed to overcapacity.” The bloc shares the Trump administration’s concerns about overcapacity, said Olof Gill, deputy chief spokesman for the the European Commission. Given the mutual concerns, the E.U. regrets “the lack of joint action” with the United States to address the problem. Just weeks ago, Greer accused the E.U. of “aggressively” supporting Airbus and said that a loan from the European Investment Bank to the French aerospace giant threatened to inject “substantial uncertainty into transatlantic trade in the aerospace sector.” The E.U. rejected Greer’s assertion, saying the loan was normal and he had “really no grounds” to question it. The bloc, made up of 27 countries, is America’s largest trading partner. Meanwhile, in August, trade talks with Canada collapsed after Prime Minister Mark Carney said the Trump administration requested “uneconomic” and unfair terms at the last minute. Carney recalled his negotiators to Ottawa and for more than three months the two sides have traded verbal barbs. Canada is the country’s third-largest trading partner, according to data through September. Recently, informal talks resumed between the U.S. and Canada but a formal deal does not yet appear to be within reach. On Wednesday, Greer said those talks with Canada were continuing, due to some outstanding “sticking points.” Another key U.S. trading partner, Mexico, was not included in Wednesday’s tariff proposals. “I think the most important one where we’re still going through the investigation process, is Mexico,” Greer told CNBC. “I think it’ll be a little bit more time before we release that report,” he said.

articles.title: Tech stocks are volatile as AI fears overshadow Huang’s Nvidia return
articles.summary: Wall Street staged a dramatic comeback Wednesday, clawing back steep morning losses as investors looked for safety in non-AI corners of the market.
articles.body: Wall Street staged a dramatic comeback Wednesday, clawing back steep morning losses as investors looked for safety in non-AI corners of the market. The tech-focused Nasdaq Composite closed lower by 0.62%, paring significant losses after falling as much as 4.6% shortly after the opening bell. The index fell for the second day in a row, resuming declines after a rebound Monday. As AI-related stocks fell, investors rushed into bonds and scooped up shares in other areas of the stock market, including materials, real estate and energy. After falling 1,100 points after the opening bell, the Dow erased those losses and gained 165 points, or 0.33%. The S&P 500 closed lower by just 0.25%, paring earlier losses, buoyed by gains in non-tech sectors. “Investors are just selling tech and fleeing for safety,” said Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management. Nvidia shares slid 3.9%. Memory-chipmakers Sandisk and Micron Technology fell 5.6% and 4.6%, respectively. Anthropic dropped almost 10% before paring losses and ending the day up by just over 1% — an outlier among AI stocks Wednesday. The AI lab on Tuesday closed below its IPO price of $83 a share for the first time, and post-debut volatility is expected. Traders for weeks now have been fretting about the AI boom and whether the vast amounts of money being spent on its buildout will pay off for companies down the line. Those fears were briefly stymied Monday, when Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, sending both the company’s shares and the broader market soaring. That relief, however, quickly faded Tuesday — with losses in tech stocks persisting Wednesday in volatile trading. Adding to the pressure were fresh data showing US economy is still running hot — prompting traders to ramp up bets on interest rate hikes — alongside new tariff proposals from President Donald Trump that have added to geopolitical uncertainty. AI nerves colliding with expectations for higher interest rates rattled markets early Wednesday. “You add the two together, and you get violent moves,” said Jamie Cox, managing partner at Harris Financial Group. Inflation data released Wednesday showed a core measure of inflation that excludes food and energy prices rose 3.3% year-over-year in October, well above the central bank’s target of 2%. Data also showed that the US economy grew much faster than anticipated last quarter, bolstering argument for the Fed to raise rates. Traders are pricing in a 97% chance that the Fed raises interest rates by a quarter point at its meeting in December, according to CME FedWatch, a real-time forecasting tool. “A December hike was already widely expected, but the bigger question now is whether the Fed sees it as enough, or signals that more tightening may be needed,” Bret Kenwell, US investment strategist at eToro, wrote in a note. Investors are already nervous about the cost of the AI buildout, especially for companies taking on debt. Higher Fed interest rates could exacerbate those costs, dimming the outlook for AI-related stocks. Data on Wednesday showed economic growth is booming, in part due to the AI buildout. Traders are also analyzing the risk that higher rates could hurt the AI boom which could inadvertently hurt the economy. The Nasdaq 100, an index including the largest tech companies, briefly fell into bear market territory on Wednesday — down 20% from its peak in early October — before paring losses. Despite the bets on the Fed raising rates, US Treasury yields were sharply lower Wednesday morning as investors nervous about the AI trade rushed into bonds. The 10-year yield declined to around 4.87%. Yields fall when bond prices rise. Wall Street’s fear gauge, the VIX, surged as high as 35 points before paring some gains. A level above 30 is associated with significant volatility. “There’s a lot of volatility, and there’s a lot of fear,” said Thomas Martin, senior portfolio manager at Globalt Investments. “It’s fear more so than fundamentals.” Investors turned to bonds as a haven, while other assets offered less protection. Gold fell below $3,500 a troy ounce and hit its lowest level in over a year before ending the day near flat. Bitcoin briefly fell below $58,000, trading near its lowest level of President Donald Trump’s second term. Stocks across Asia and Europe were, too, mostly in the red as anxiety about AI rippled through global markets. South Korea’s Kospi, dominated by memory chip giants SK Hynix and Samsung, led the losses for major indexes, closing down 6.2%. The Kospi has plunged 48% since a peak in June. Europe’s benchmark Stoxx 600 index lost a little more than 1%. Nvidia shares soared more than 30% Monday to score their third-best day on record after the company announced it had reinstated Huang as CEO and president, effective immediately. Huang was brought back just 11 days after he stepped down following reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman who US officials feared could be working with Chinese intelligence and another with a direct subordinate. The announcement turbocharged an already buoyant day for stocks — but the upward swing didn’t last long. Investors have since returned to dumping tech stocks, fueled by concerns over the durability of the AI frenzy. “We are not out of the woods with the downside risk from the AI trade,” Chris Brigati, chief investment officer at SWBC, wrote in a note. “Investors are still nervous and none of the fundamental questions about AI’s return on investment from the heavy capex spending have been resolved even with the unusual return of Jensen as CEO of Nvidia.” Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO last week did little to quell investor concerns about potential regulation and a slowdown in AI investment, particularly for data centers.

articles.title: The $2 trillion chip rally is unraveling — here's what history says comes next
articles.summary: Two days after Nvidia's record rebound, chip stocks are back where they started.
articles.body:
The biggest one-day rescue in stock market history is coming undone. Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia, and Wall Street's AI doubts are back with a vengeance.

Monday was supposed to be the start of the comeback. Nvidia's ( NVDA ) board brought Huang back at the White House's urging a week after chip stocks' worst week since 2001 , and the group added about $2 trillion in a day , a record $950 billion of it from Nvidia alone.

The sell-off since has hit the whole sector. The PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) sank nearly 8% Tuesday, with Micron ( MU ), AMD ( AMD ), and Intel ( INTC ) down roughly 8% to 11% and Broadcom ( AVGO ) and Taiwan Semiconductor ( TSM ) off about 4%. On Wednesday, the index briefly dropped below last Friday's low, as Nvidia and Micron fell as much as 9% and 13%, before buyers stepped in and cut its loss to less than 1%.

The pain spread Wednesday morning, when the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) fell more than 3% and the Nasdaq 100 ( ^NDX ) nearly 5%. Dip buyers pushed both indexes back to small losses by the close, though Alphabet ( GOOG , GOOGL ), Microsoft ( MSFT ) and Amazon ( AMZN ) still finished lower.

Huang's return settled the question of who runs Nvidia. It didn't answer whether the debt-fueled AI-building boom will pay off, with tech borrowing costs climbing and the Fed still expected to raise rates on Dec. 9.

Sherwood News' Luke Kawa doesn't blame any single headline. "I think you can pin it on the sum of all the things that everyone's been pointing to for a while," he said on Yahoo Finance's Market Hang Tuesday.

Washington wants to help. President Trump told the New York Post a pardon for Huang is " always an option , I guess, but I don't think it'll be necessary." Asked about a government stake in Nvidia, he said, "It's probably not too late."

"I question what kind of a put it is," GammaRoad Capital Partners chief investment officer Jordan Rizzuto said. "I think it may be a very short-term put." Wednesday's new tariff proposal barely moved futures.

Turnaround Tuesday showed up on schedule. The next part of the script leans bearish. In the 20 times since 1993 that the SPDR S&P 500 ETF ( SPY ) opened a Monday 2% or more higher, it gave back at least half of that gain by Wednesday's close only five times, according to Yahoo Finance calculations. SPY was on pace to join them Wednesday morning before a late rebound kept it out.

Every one of those fades went on to break the prior Friday's low within three months, most of them within a week. Of the 15 bounces that held up, only a third eventually broke the low in that span. Three of the drops came in the fall of 2008.

articles.title: Market sell-off eases up, but AI doubts, tariffs and inflation still weigh down stocks
articles.summary: U.S. stocks broadly slumped Wednesday, led by companies linked to the AI boom.
articles.body: U.S. stocks broadly slumped Wednesday, led by companies linked to the AI boom. The volatile day began with a sharp sell-off that briefly sent the influential Nasdaq 100 index into bear market territory, which occurs when an index falls by 20% or more from its most recent high. The S&P 500 was down by as much as 3.2% in early trading. But sentiment among traders and investors improved slightly over the course of the day. An early beneficiary of the renewed optimism was Anthropic, the AI giant that staged a record-setting IPO last week, only to see its stock battered for three straight trading sessions. Shortly after midday, Anthropic was finally trading back above its IPO price of $83 per share. Meanwhile, the Nasdaq Composite was down roughly 1.5% and the S&P 500 was lower by only 0.5%. The Dow was flat in early afternoon trading and just barely back over a symbolic 50,000. Nvidia lags behind Even as markets pulled back from their lows, Nvidia remained among the biggest losers in key indexes. After soaring by 31% on Monday on news that its recently-departed CEO Jensen Huang would return to the C-suite, the stock was still lower by about 7% Wednesday, its second straight down day. The return of Huang, a de facto ambassador for the artificial intelligence industry, briefly reassured investors that big AI firms, and the trillions of dollars they borrow and lend, would continue to grow without interruption. Stock markets Monday staged their biggest one-day rally since April 2025, as the Nasdaq 100 skyrocketed 6.8% and the S&P 500 surged 4.7%. President Donald Trump pushed Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang over the weekend despite multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy. Before the president stepped in, the board had been unequivocal that it did not plan to reinstate Huang. Trump said Monday that he “probably” decided to intervene in Nvidia’s internal leadership decision because he was concerned about a market sell-off in the week after Huang’s departure fueled partly by investor concerns about how the CEO’s resignation would impact the broader AI industry. But ever since Monday’s rally, markets have struggled to maintain that upward momentum. “The risk-off tone has returned over the last 24 hours, as Monday’s rebound in tech stocks lost momentum once again,” Deutsche Bank strategists said in a note early Wednesday. Before Monday’s one-day rally, stocks had faced weeks of selling, which pushed the Nasdaq 100 into correction territory on Friday, which is defined as a 10% drop from its last high. Shares of semiconductor stocks, as tracked by the Philadelphia semiconductor index, have plunged more than 40% since their last peak in June. Stocks of companies that make data center and computer memory products have plummeted 60% over the same period. AI-related sentiment has also been damaged further by frontier developer Anthropic, whose shares have spiraled lower since its initial public offering last week. Stocks Wednesday likely faced additional pressure due to the looming Thanksgiving holiday. U.S. markets will be closed Thursday and open for only a half-day of trading Friday. Investors are more likely to cut their large or risky trades before extended weekends, in order to avoid being trapped in positions while events unfold. New tariffs fuel uncertainty On top of cracks in the AI sector, “matters weren’t helped by the latest tariff headlines,” Deutsche Bank’s team wrote. On Wednesday, the Trump administration unveiled a new wave of tariffs on the United States’ top trading partners, such as the European Union, China, Japan and a dozen more. “It is another reminder that while the legal justification for tariffs keeps changing, US protectionism is becoming increasingly difficult to unwind,” ING senior trade economist Inga Fechner wrote in a note Wednesday. That drove stocks down further, with the prospect that more tariffs could cause renewed trade tensions, a renewed inflation spike and cause a flare-up with a policy that had largely started to subside in recent months. Even before Wednesday’s formal announcement, a spokesperson for the Chinese Commerce Ministry blasted the new import duties. “Tariff wars and trade wars are in the interests of neither side,” the spokesperson said. The ministry called it “political manipulation.” “Some investors might have been caught off guard by news that the Administration is on track to release more tariffs, but the key question about the Administration unveiling new tariffs from the Section 301 overcapacity investigation has never been an issue of whether but when,” wrote Sarah Bianchi, chief strategist of international political affairs at Evercore ISI. Inflation is still climbing Compounding the negative pressure facing investors Wednesday, the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge moved further away from its 2% goal. The personal consumption expenditures index was 3.8% for October, up from 3.6% in September. Even excluding food and energy, the “core” inflation reading rose to 3.3%. It had been 3.1% the previous month. The rise in core inflation readings is particularly noteworthy because it can indicate that higher gas prices sparked by the Iran war are spilling over into the rest of the economy. It also raises the likelihood that the Fed will raise interest rates at its next meeting, which concludes with a rate decision Dec. 9. Last week, a top Fed policymaker said the central bank needed to “shock people” with a larger rate hike than is typical. “I’m very, very concerned about inflation,” Fed governor Christopher Waller said in a CNBC interview. “It’s kind of headed in the wrong direction, and it’s spreading out.” Waller said the Fed needed to take “more aggressive actions,” such as hiking by 0.50%, more than the Fed’s usual 0.25% rate increase. “You might need to, like, shock people,” he said. A rate hike would carry its own complications, however. As trillion-dollar tech giants borrow hundreds of billions of dollars to build out AI data centers and chips, any increase to interest rates could quickly raise their massive costs. It could also hurt an already pained U.S. consumer. Mortgage rates continue to hover well above 7%, and a rate hike could push borrowing costs higher for auto loans, credit cards, personal loans and other forms of credit.

articles.title: Fresh 25% Trump tariff threat with a carrot of 17% duty: What it means for India
articles.summary: Amid the India-US trade deal negotiations, the Donald Trump administration unveiled a fresh set of tariffs aimed at a host of countries including India.
articles.body: Amid the India-US trade deal negotiations, the Donald Trump administration unveiled a fresh set of tariffs aimed at a host of countries including India.The proposed tariffs, for which several countries have been targeted, form a part of the United States Trade Representative's (USTR) Section 301 investigations into structural excess capacity.China faces the hardest hit with a potential final tariff rate of up to 45% for some of its goods.In India’s case the tariffs could go up to as high as 25%. The twist is the prospect of lower tariffs if a trade deal is finalised.What has the Donald Trump administration announced? Why has India been selected among the list of countries subject to fresh tariffs? And what does it mean for trade deal talks and India’s export prospects?What Trump administration has announcedThe Trump administration has announced that the tariffs on India could range from 17-25% depending on the finalisation of a trade deal between the two countries.Up to 25% tariffs on all goods from India, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods would be applicable, but there is also the prospect of 17% tariffs if a trade deal is agreed on.“The Trade Representative further proposes to consider whether the additional duties applied should be adjusted to account for, among others, duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions, or were India to reach an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade with the United States that is responsive to the determinations in this investigation into the acts, policies, and practices of India, a tariff rate of 17 percent,” the USTR release reads.It’s also important to note that the new tariffs will not be levied on top of any existing tariffs that are applicable to specific sectors.For many months now, the USTR's office has been examining whether 16 countries follow policies that encourage excess capacity production. Such practices can push prices down and undermine US industries, according to the investigation.Interestingly, the probe came on the back of the US Supreme Court's decision to overturn the Trump administration's reciprocal tariffs and was widely seen as an alternative way for the government to keep the tariff pressure on the country’s trading partners.Following the US apex court ruling, the USTR had launched two investigations under Section 301. While one covered about a hundred countries, over alleged violations of export regulations relating to forced labour, the other targeted 16 economies over policies aimed at encouraging excess production.Why these tariffs on India?Because the US claims that it has found India among many countries indulging in what it claims are unreasonable acts, policies and practices. The US has identified five areas that it sees as practices that end up being detrimental to US interests:Industrial plans aimed at expanding manufacturingInsufficient labour protectionsPolicies involving financial repressionPersistent barriers to market access; andFailure to tackle global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies.According to the assessment, these acts, policies and practices place a burden on or restrict US commerce in three ways. They limit business opportunities for US producers and exporters in India and other countries; damage the US economy by contributing to declines in domestic manufacturing output, exports, employment and investment; and heighten economic security risks for the US, including through dependence on inputs from non-market economies.According to the Trump administration, these concerns are particularly significant in sectors such as healthcare, including pharmaceuticals and medical devices, as well as steel, solar energy and information and communications technology (ICT).What it means for India and trade deal talks with USThe step assumes significance because the India-US trade deal is yet to be finalised. Despite repeated statements from both sides on talks being in final stages, no deal has yet been announced. In February this year, the US announced an 18% tariff on India after imposing 50% duties in August 2025. However, with the US Supreme Court ruling that reciprocal tariffs are illegal, India continued to face low tariffs like all other countries.India has time and again said that a trade deal will be finalised once it gets a favourable tariff rate compared to its competitors. Now, with the US adding pressure of up to 25% tariffs in the absence of a trade deal, it remains to be seen whether talks will be expedited.Manoj Mishra, Partner and Tax Controversy Management Leader, Grant Thornton Bharat believes that the proposed US tariffs of up to 25% on Indian goods, net of existing Section 301 tariffs and subject to certain exemptions, could pose fresh challenges for Indian exporters.“The USTR’s scrutiny of India’s Make in India, PLI and Atmanirbhar Bharat initiatives, particularly in the steel, solar, pharmaceuticals and electronics sectors, has wider implications for India’s manufacturing ambitions,” he tells TOI.According to Mishra, the proposed tariffs could increase landed costs, erode export competitiveness, compress margins and impact manufacturing investments.But, what does it mean for trade deal talks?“The possibility of a lower tariff rate of 17%, contingent upon India concluding an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade with the US that addresses the investigation findings, underscores the need to expedite bilateral trade negotiations,” Mishra says.“To mitigate the impact, India could leverage its expanding network of FTAs, explore alternative export markets and diversify global supply chains to reduce dependence on the US market,” he adds.Ajay Srivastava, founder of Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI) points out that under the proposal, India’s exports get a calculated 1% edge over Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Thailand (18% deal rate) and a 3% edge over Vietnam and China (20% deal rate).“By deploying a dual-rate structure - threatening steep baseline tariffs against countries that refuse a pact while offering lower rates to those that sign - Washington reclaims the bargaining power to impose duties at will and extract unilateral concessions, allowing a government to secure tariff relief even if the industrial capacity that prompted the investigation remains unchanged,” he opines.“Because these manipulated rates are a deliberate bait to extract one-sided concessions - and with the threat of Graham tariffs of up to 100% still hanging over it - India must reject the trade deal and instead answer the allegations sector by sector, showing that its investment serves domestic buyers, overseas customers, and future demand rather than letting exports alone be treated as proof of excess capacity,” Srivastava says.Agneshwar Sen, Trade Policy Leader, EY India believes that the proposed tariffs reinforce the broader shift towards a more protectionist global trade environment.“For India, the key priority will be to preserve competitiveness and market access in the US while continuing to diversify export markets and strengthen domestic manufacturing capabilities,” he tells TOI.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: Rupee recovers FY26 losses, strengthens to 92.16 against dollar on equity rally
articles.summary: The Indian rupee strengthened sharply on Wednesday, rising 69 paise to close at 92.16 (provisional) against the US dollar, its strongest level so far this
articles.body: The Indian rupee strengthened sharply on Wednesday, rising 69 paise to close at 92.16 (provisional) against the US dollar, its strongest level so far this year, as robust buying in domestic equities and sustained foreign fund inflows supported the currency.Forex traders said lower crude oil prices also helped the rupee recover all its losses recorded during the current financial year, while global investors increasingly favoured Indian equities over other assets.At the interbank foreign exchange market, the rupee opened at 92.65 against the dollar before climbing to 92.16 by the end of the session. The currency had last closed at a stronger level of 92.28 on March 16 this year.The latest gain followed a 23-paise decline on Monday, when the rupee settled at 92.85 after retreating from a seven-month high.The currency market remained closed on Tuesday on account of Prakash Gurpurb Sri Guru Nanak Dev.The rupee has gained more than 1.6% over five consecutive sessions since November 13, when it closed at 94.19 against the dollar. Over the past seven weeks, it has recovered nearly 5% from its record low closing level of 96.88, recorded on October 8.Foreign inflows, lower crude support recoveryAnuj Choudhary, research analyst at Mirae Asset Sharekhan, attributed Wednesday's appreciation to the surge in domestic equity markets and weaker crude oil prices. He said a strong dollar, however, limited the rupee's gains.Choudhary expects the currency to maintain a positive bias, supported by strength in domestic markets and foreign institutional investor (FII) inflows."Traders may take cues from GDP, weekly unemployment claims and durable goods orders data from the US. USD-INR spot price is expected to trade in a range of Rs 91.95 to Rs 92.55," he said, as quoted by news agency PTI.Kaveri More, commodity technical analyst at Choice Broking, said the rupee's rebound could extend further, with the next downside targets around 91.40-90."The rally is supported by strong foreign portfolio inflows of over $4 billion in November, renewed foreign bond purchases, easing crude oil prices and measures undertaken by the RBI to improve dollar liquidity and stabilise the currency," More said.She added that sustained foreign inflows and softer crude prices could remain key factors supporting the currency's recovery in the near term.Rajeev Sharan, head of research at Brickwork Ratings, said foreign funds had shifted towards Indian equities as investors moved away from AI-heavy markets such as South Korea, Taiwan and Japan.He said foreign funds had poured a record more than USD 12 billion into Indian equities in November. Along with Brent crude slipping below USD 90 a barrel, these inflows outweighed the dollar index remaining close to 104.RBI's dollar purchases and market movementThe Reserve Bank of India (RBI) purchased a net $6.936 billion in the spot currency market in September, according to its monthly bulletin released on Wednesday. The amount was substantially lower than the net USD 43.264 billion purchased in August.September marked the fourth consecutive month of net dollar purchases by the central bank.According to data compiled by PTI, the RBI bought $18.652 billion in July and $561 million in June, while recording an outflow of $6.104 billion in May.On a gross basis, the RBI purchased $82.181 billion and sold $75.245 billion in September.The central bank said the rupee had depreciated in early October amid a stronger US dollar and rising crude oil prices, before reversing direction. Its recovery was supported by RBI measures to curb speculative dollar demand, softer crude prices and renewed portfolio inflows in November up to November 19.Meanwhile, the dollar index, which measures the US currency against a basket of six major currencies, stood at 103.90, up 0.15%.Brent crude futures were trading 0.16% lower at $91.55 per barrel.Domestic equities also recorded strong gains. The BSE Sensex was up 1,215.02 points, or 1.47%, at 83,651.01 in afternoon trade, while the NSE Nifty gained 368.15 points, or 1.45%, to 25,717.60. During the session, the Sensex touched a high of 84,498.21, while the Nifty climbed to 25,951.65.The gains came after both benchmark indices had ended nearly 2% lower in the previous session.Despite that decline, foreign institutional investors were net buyers of Indian equities worth Rs 5,672.99 crore on Monday, according to exchange data.Money habits form by age 7.
