articles.title: FAA's 'line up and wait' rule is in effect: How it could affect your flight
articles.summary: Heading to the airport? Here's what the FAA's "line up and wait" rule could mean for your travel plans.
articles.body:
Some offers on this page are from advertisers who pay us, which may affect which products we write about, but not our recommendations. See our Advertiser Disclosure .

The Federal Aviation Administration has restricted a takeoff protocol that could potentially slow holiday travel. The FAA has modified the "line up and wait" procedure that allows departing planes to taxi to a runway and remain in queue for takeoff. The maneuver helps expedite flight operations but has been revised due to staffing concerns.

The change took effect Tuesday, Nov. 24, as an estimated 417,000 flights began to take to the air for the nine-day Thanksgiving travel period. Under the stricter guidelines, a dedicated air traffic control supervisor must be available to coordinate line up and wait operations, rather than having air traffic controllers multitask.

"The purpose of this change is to elevate the safety standard for Line Up and Wait (LUAW) operations by removing ambiguity in staffing requirements," the FAA notice said. The enhanced policy ensures that a supervisor or controller is "fully available to oversee the safety of the operation without the distraction of simultaneously managing other operational tasks."

The stricter guidance could impact takeoff operations at understaffed facilities, and is slated to remain in effect until June 9, 2027.

Weather delays, heavy traffic, and staffing concerns

Brian Cohen, a travel writer at " The Gate ," said that "the timing of the rule being placed into effect could have been better, as it could cause delays and even cancellations of flights during the busiest travel period of the year."

Adding the FAA's decision to enforce the rule to the pressing holiday crowds, the threat of bad weather in large swaths of the nation, and recent technical glitches, all increase "the chances of your travel plans being interrupted," Cohen wrote.

He suggests travelers frequently check the latest flight updates during the holiday rush.

On Monday, a temporary ground stop at Chicago's O'Hare International Airport was blamed on a staffing shortage. More than 170 flights were delayed as the Thanksgiving travel season began.

The FAA launched a recruitment campaign this year to bolster staffing, with an estimated 1,500 positions currently unfilled. An expected loss of 5,307 controllers is forecast over the next three years due to attrition, the agency says.

'Unprecedented action' to limit delays and cancellations

In a statement Tuesday regarding holiday travel, U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy said that government officials are working to "predict and address congestion in the airspace" and have "taken unprecedented action to limit flight delays and cancellations."

The FAA recommends that air travelers check nasstatus.faa.gov for real-time airport conditions to see how weather may affect their flights. The Department of Transportation also provides information related to airline policies regarding delays and flight cancellations .

articles.title: 2026 was a huge year for data center power. 2028 could be nearly 3 times bigger.
articles.summary: A new report from Goldman Sachs Research estimates that the US will add about 52 gigawatts of data center power capacity in 2028.
articles.body:
Think this year's been a big one for data centers and their relentless power demands? Wait until you get a load of 2028.

A new report from Goldman Sachs Research estimates that the US will add about 52 gigawatts of data center power capacity in 2028 — nearly triple the 18 gigawatts expected this year and more than five times last year's additions. That's after data center power capacity and demand grew nearly 30% year over year so far in 2026, with data centers accounting for more than a third of all US power demand growth.

The forecast suggests that many of the issues associated with the AI boom — from rising electricity bills to competition for power and growing community opposition to data centers — could get considerably worse before the decade is out.

It's not just that tech companies are building more data centers. They're building bigger and more power-hungry ones. Goldman expects the average power capacity of a US data center building to reach 49 megawatts in 2028, up from 31 this year and 16 in 2020. The growth is also expected to be highly concentrated geographically. Virginia and Texas alone are projected to account for 36% of new US data center power capacity in 2028.

The projected growth in 2028 far exceeds the assumptions underpinning Goldman's existing natural gas outlook, which anticipates average annual data center power capacity additions of 28 gigawatts from 2027 through 2035. The analysts said the new estimates reinforced their bullish outlook for US natural gas prices through 2030.

But that growth isn't guaranteed. While Goldman's estimates already account for historical rates of project delays and cancellations, roughly half of the data center power capacity expected to come online in 2028 isn't yet under construction. The analysts warned that political changes following the midterm elections, as well as growing local opposition to data centers, could lead to more project delays and cancellations than expected.

In other words, the AI industry's appetite for power is growing just as political tolerance for that appetite is being tested.

articles.title: ‘One Air India Group:’ New CEO focuses on synergy to cut losses, improve operations
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Air India’s new CEO Tewolde Gebremariam will implement a “One AI Group” approach for greater synergy between full cost AI and its budget arm AI
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Air India’s new CEO Tewolde Gebremariam will implement a “One AI Group” approach for greater synergy between full cost AI and its budget arm AI Express in a bid to cut spiralling losses that have touched almost Rs 60,000 crore since Jan 2022 when Tata took over the two airlines. And also to meet operational challenges.While the airlines will operate under their own licences and have post holders as required by law, there will be a significant rejig that will see dual reporting with “people and teams working as one group, drawing on the best capabilities and expertise across both airlines.”Customer-facing, operational and regulatory functions will remain airline-centric, while enabling functions such as finance, HR, IT and centres of excellence will increasingly be managed at a group level. “People and teams will work as one group, drawing on the best capabilities and expertise across both airlines. The aim is to generate synergies,” Gebremariam said at a Town Hall Wednesday.He conveyed his blue print for flying AI Group out of turbulence, which the full service arm has been grappling with both on the financial and operational fronts. A new organisational structure will be finalised shortly, with two new roles being added to the core management team — group strategy officer and chief of training academy. Deepak Rajawat, Air India Express CFO who will take over as the budget arm’s CEO on Dec 1, 2026, will be a part of the management team.Setting operational excellence, profitability, growth and closer integration across the group as his priorities, the CEO stressed on the deliverables: safe and clean aircraft, on-time flights, reliable baggage handling, and customer-friendly service. He said on time performance has improved in the last three months with domestic operations of both AI and AI Express achieving OTP above 80%. While long haul international performance is improving, it remains a key area of focus.Tewolde emphasised that restoring profitability remains a top priority, particularly amid industry-wide cost pressures including higher fuel costs and continuing operational challenges arising from regional airspace restrictions. “Cost discipline is not a one-time exercise. It must become part of our culture,” he told employees.“Oct and Nov have been encouraging. In some areas, load factors have grown, while in others yields have improved. Overall, (revenue) is increasing. We are making progress,” he said.Factoring in geopolitical challenges, AI is rejigging its network by moving more westbound connecting traffic through Mumbai, which is less affected by airspace closures. Delhi will increasingly support eastbound connecting flows. “We can't control the external environment. What we can do is build an airline that is resilient in all conditions, can withstand challenges and continue to succeed. We need to make ourselves stronger every day,” he said.While acknowledging the industry's current challenges, including geopolitical tensions, airspace closures and elevated fuel costs, he said Air India's long-term outlook remains strong. "We must keep one eye firmly on today's challenges and another on tomorrow's opportunities," he told employees. The CEO identified cost consciousness, accountability and what he called "constructive impatience" as critical attributes for AI’s next phase of growth.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: CoreWeave’s Banks to Sell $4.5 Billion Meta-Tied Loan Next Week
articles.summary: CoreWeave Inc.’s bankers at Morgan Stanley and Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group Inc. are preparing a $4.5 billion loan sale for as soon as next week, with the...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- CoreWeave Inc.'s bankers at Morgan Stanley and Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group Inc. are preparing a $4.5 billion loan sale for as soon as next week, with the financing secured by graphics processing units for Meta Platforms Inc.

CoreWeave can draw on the proceeds of this debt sale from an escrow account that will fund GPUs for a data center in Dalton, Georgia, according to people with knowledge of the matter. The debt is expected to be paid down gradually over the life of the loan, the people said, asking not to be identified as the details are private.

The debt sale from the junk-rated neocloud was already expected to carry investment-grade ratings, thanks to its contract with Meta. But it's coming at a challenging time, with CoreWeave one of the companies at the heart of investor concerns about the potential payoff from the massive spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure. Adding to the worries, billions of dollars in loans tied to Chinese firms are now on pause, as new US curbs on chip access threatens Asia's burgeoning AI debt financing market.

CoreWeave helped soothe nerves briefly earlier this month when its full-year revenue exceeded both its previous forecast and Wall Street's average estimate, but on Wednesday, the cost to protect the company's debt against default for five years increased by the most ever. The swaps are pricing in a more than 70% chance of default within the next half-decade.

CoreWeave's 9% bond due in 2031 was trading at record lows to yield 18% on Wednesday, according to Trace. That's paying more than double what the loan transaction could yield, with initial discussions focusing around 7% to 7.5%, the people with knowledge said. Still, potential investors have already registered indications of interest in line with the transaction size, one of the people said. The company's delayed draw term loans are trading around par, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

Details and timing of the deal are still being finalized and could change, the people said.

Representatives for CoreWeave and Morgan Stanley declined to comment, while spokespeople for MUFG and Meta didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.

articles.title: China added nearly 10 times more power capacity than the US in 2025 as the AI race heats up
articles.summary: While the US fights to maintain an edge in computing advancement, China has pulled far ahead in power capacity generation.
articles.body:
While Washington has wrestled with the national security implications of China's access to Nvidia's ( NVDA ) advanced semiconductors — concerns brought into sharp relief by Jensen Huang's ouster and subsequent reinstatement as CEO — Beijing has been building out its electrical infrastructure at a speed far outpacing the US.

As China ramps up its AI ambitions and seeks to keep pace with the US, the nation has built roughly 550 gigawatts of power capacity in 2025, nearly triple its pace in 2022 and nearly 10 times what the US installed in 2025, per data from Apollo Global chief economist Torsten Sløk. (Disclosure: Yahoo is a portfolio company of funds managed by affiliates of Apollo Global Management.)

The gap between the US and China's power installation, Sløk said, "has widened every year since 2022 as the AI-driven race for electricity heats up."

The US maintains a clear edge in raw AI computing power, driven primarily by the most advanced chips made by Nvidia. Those chips have been subject to export restrictions since 2022, brought to light by the Huang scandal, and Congress is now considering several bills that tighten export controls even further.

In the meantime, Beijing has pushed Chinese companies to develop their own systems, the most notable of which have been produced by Huawei, which was found guilty in a US court on Tuesday of conspiracy to steal trade secrets . While Huawei's semiconductors have become critical to China's AI industry and to buyers abroad who can't afford or can't access Nvidia's chips, experts say their technology continues to lag that of Nvidia.

The power of a semiconductor is relatively unimportant, however, if there's no electricity to power the data center that hosts it — a major bottleneck in the US push for AI dominance.

As demand for power has surged in the US, power capacity in the US has climbed as well. The country added 53 gigawatts of new electricity generation capacity in 2025, according to data from the Energy Information Administration. Power capacity specifically for data centers expanded by 12 gigawatts year-on-year from Jan. 1 to late November.

Running those numbers forward, country-wide data center power capacity could reach 92 gigawatts by the end of 2027, per Goldman Sachs analysts Hongcen Wei, Daan Struyven, and Samantha Dart, with an additional 52 gigawatts likely to come online in 2028.

Yet that pace remains far behind the hundreds of gigawatts per year China has been installing through the past five years. That's a problem for the US' ambition toward AI dominance, Thomas Healy, CEO of energy technology company Hyliion, told Yahoo Finance.

articles.title: Russian oil firm Lukoil’s overseas assets sold to investors led by US billionaire Todd Boehly
articles.summary: The deal will result in the US government receiving an equity stake in Lukoil via the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation.
articles.body: US billionaire Todd Boehly is leading a consortium to acquire the vast portfolio of international energy assets belonging to Russia’s second-largest oil producer, his investment firm Eldridge announced Wednesday. Eldridge said in a statement that the consortium, which includes the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation, had agreed to buy Lukoil International from its sanctioned Russian parent. The sale price was not disclosed, but the deal will result in the US government receiving an equity stake in Lukoil via the DFC. The deal will “secure critical global energy assets under American and allied ownership,” the statement added. Lukoil’s upstream operations span 11 countries and currently produce around 350,000 barrels of oil equivalent a day. The portfolio includes oil and gas fields; three refineries in Europe; 2,000 retail gas stations across 16 countries in Europe, North America and Central Asia; and an international trading business. Lukoil’s overseas portfolio of assets will be acquired via a share swap, with restricted shares in its Russian parent and other Russian companies exchanged for Lukoil International’s equity. This “avoids any direct cash payment to Russia under the transaction,” Eldridge said. Other investment partners include UAE-based Catena Investment Holding and US investment bank Xtellus Partners. The transaction is subject to conditional approval from the US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control. CNN has contacted Lukoil and the DFC for comment. Petras Katinas, a research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a defense and security think tank in London, argued that the deal “demonstrates the efficiency of sanctions.” “Western sanctions are forcing one of Russia’s largest oil companies to relinquish international assets accumulated over decades,” Katinas told CNN earlier this month, ahead of the deal being announced. Transferring refineries and fuel stations to non-Russian owners will “reduce Moscow’s trade influence over important energy infrastructure and remove a source of future earnings for Lukoil,” he added. The deal caps a long and tumultuous sale process. Lukoil put its international assets up for sale more than a year ago after the Treasury Department sanctioned the company in a bid to pressure Moscow to end its war in Ukraine by cutting off an important source of revenue. Rosneft, Russia’s top oil producer, was also sanctioned at the time. The months that followed saw potential deals come and go. Last year, Swiss commodities trading firm Gunvor Group, now Centalion, made an offer for the assets—though the deal was scuttled when it could not win approval from the Treasury. Then, in January, private equity firm Carlyle agreed to buy the foreign assets, excluding those in Kazakhstan. That deal also fell apart this year. The transaction is an unusual investment for Boehly, a part-owner of sports teams including the Los Angeles Dodgers and Los Angeles Lakers. Boehly’s asset management and insurance holding company Eldridge, which manages more than $75 billion in assets, is focused mostly on sports, entertainment, diversified credit and real estate.

articles.title: Precio de la luz por horas mañana, jueves 26 de noviembre: cuándo es más barata y más cara en el día
articles.standfirst: El precio de la luz baja 15,79€ este jueves
articles.summary: El precio de la luz baja 15,79€ este jueves
articles.body: Hoy, el precio medio de la electricidad se sitúa en 194,35 €/MWh, lo que representa una bajada de 15,79 € en comparación con el día anterior, que cerró en 210,14 €/MWh. Este jueves, los consumidores deben estar atentos a las horas más caras y más baratas para gestionar mejor su consumo eléctrico. Los momentos más caros para consumir electricidad se concentran especialmente entre las 19:00 y las 23:00, con picos notables de precios. Durante el periodo de mayor demanda, se identifica un bloque continuo que va desde las 08:00, alcanzando un valor de 214.06 €/MWh, hasta las 20:00 con 275.52 €/MWh. Este tramo se caracteriza por precios que superan los 260 €/MWh, siendo la franja horaria entre las 20:00 y las 22:00 especialmente costosa. Además, el último pico destacado se registra a las 00:00 con 231.42 €/MWh, lo que indica una persistencia de tarifas elevadas en las horas de mayor consumo. La luz es más barata durante el mediodía, lo que representa una excelente oportunidad de ahorro. Entre las 12:00 - 13:00 (118.10 €/MWh) y 14:00 - 15:00 (117.06 €/MWh), se observan precios bajos, con la franja más económica situada entre 13:00 - 14:00 (110.03 €/MWh) y 22:00 - 23:00 (199.58 €/MWh). En el análisis de las franjas horarias de hoy, destaca una amplia diferencia entre la hora más cara y la más barata, que alcanza los 165,49 €/MWh, lo que subraya la importancia de planificar el consumo eléctrico para maximizar el ahorro. Esta volatilidad sugiere que la gestión inteligente de la demanda puede suponer un gran beneficio económico para los consumidores a lo largo del día.

articles.title: Citadel to Hand Back $3.5 Billion of Gains This Year to Clients
articles.summary: Ken Griffin’s Citadel will hand some of the profits it has generated this year back to clients, continuing its tradition of returning capital to restrict the...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Ken Griffin's Citadel will hand some of the profits it has generated this year back to clients, continuing its tradition of returning capital to restrict the amount of money it manages.

The hedge fund firm is expected to return about $3.5 billion and potentially more, according to people with knowledge of the matter. Investors will see about half of their net profits returned to them, one of the people said, asking not to be identified because the details are private.

Citadel's flagship Wellington fund gained 1.7% in October after avoiding the losses suffered by a number of its peers, driving year-to-date gains to 15.3%. The firm managed $78 billion at the start of November, according to its website.

A representative for the investment firm declined to comment.

Citadel has regularly returned profits back to investors — a total of about $33 billion from 2017 through 2025 — and hasn't been actively raising money. Peers such as D.E. Shaw & Co. and Point72 Asset Management have also given back billions of dollars to clients in recent years. Hedge funds often take such steps to control their assets and avoid harming returns.

These measures make it even harder for investors to gain exposure to hedge funds, with demand for the asset class at unprecedented levels and only a handful of big funds looking to bring in fresh money.

articles.title: Why Nvidia's 'Jensen put' failed to stop the AI trade meltdown
articles.summary: Jensen Huang's return as CEO on Monday may have temporarily stabilized the AI trade, but it did little to fix the broader financial pressures weighing on mar...
articles.body:
Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO on Monday may have temporarily stabilized the AI trade, but it did little to fix the broader financial pressures weighing on markets.

Stock losses accelerated on Wednesday as Wall Street renewed its nervousness about the AI trade. Nvidia's ( NVDA ) shares tanked 6%, extending losses for a second consecutive session .

"It simply feels bad out there, and I'm not sure who's there to kick-save things at this current juncture into holiday illiquidity and zero tolerance for losses," Charlie McElligott, cross-asset macro strategist at Nomura, wrote in a note on Wednesday.

McElligott pointed out that the so-called Jensen put, or the idea that Huang's return can support the chip giant and the broader AI trade, does not address the tightening financial conditions in markets.

"What did Monday change? Not much!" the strategist said.

On Monday, President Trump said he spoke to Nvidia's board members and "convinced" them to reinstate Huang 11 days after the CEO resigned amid reports of his affairs, including with a suspected Chinese spy. Nvidia stock and the rest of the chip sector rallied hard on the announcement.

Despite the reinstatement, McElligott pointed to broader pressures facing markets, including higher interest rates, wider credit spreads, and heightened volatility, prompting investors to flock to cash and US Treasurys.

A squeeze on financial conditions leaves Nvidia and the broader AI trade vulnerable if another major setback emerges. According to an anonymous investor cited by McElligott, Huang's return has raised the stakes given greater scrutiny and congressional inquiries over the AI chip giant.

"This absolutely HAS to work," the investor said. "By that I mean he (Jensen) has to be 100% clean."

In other words, "if NVDA were to 'Go Wrong' again, we are left with an even higher cliff to jump from," McElligott wrote.

The AI trade has taken a substantial hit over the past month, with nearly every corner of the industry tumbling substantially. Nvidia stock is down roughly 30% over the past month and roughly 21% year to date.

Memory chipmaker Micron Technology ( MU ) is roughly 50% off its all-time high hit over the summer. Storage and memory-related stock Sandisk ( SNDK ) is down roughly 70% from its June record high.

articles.title: World reacts to Trump’s new tariffs as US stocks tumble
articles.summary: The new levies come after an eight-month investigation launched by the United States Trade Representative.
articles.body:
The Trump administration has announced new tariffs on 14 major trading partners , including China and the European Union, claiming that excess production has given them an unfair advantage.

The proposed levies come after a months-long investigation into the trade practices of 12 countries, the 27-member EU and the self-governing island of Taiwan, launched after the Supreme Court struck down United States President Donald Trump’s sweeping global tariffs in February.

The highest tariff rate announced on Wednesday would hit China the hardest, at 20 percent, adding to the roughly 25 percent duties that Trump imposed on China during his first term.

The proposed tariffs would not apply to about $30bn of Chinese imports under consideration for tariff reductions through a bilateral mechanism known as the Board of Trade.

Washington has long accused China of subsidising its industries and flooding global markets with low-cost exports ranging from steel to electric vehicles and solar products, allegations that Beijing has once again denied.

“The so-called ‘overcapacity’ is a false issue, and China opposes using it as an excuse for political manipulation,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said, urging the world’s two top economies to maintain stable relations.

Other US trading partners facing proposed new tariffs include India, Japan, South Korea, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.

Mexico and Norway were also part of the probe but were excluded from the new round of tariffs because investigations into their trade practices are still ongoing.

The tariff announcement follows an eight-month investigation initiated by US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, under Section 301 of the US Trade Act of 1974, which permits the president to impose import taxes and other sanctions against countries found to engage in unreasonable or discriminatory trade practices.

“The administration’s use of Section 301 is cynical,” Gregory Shaffer, professor of international law at the Georgetown University Law Center, told Al Jazeera. “It launched these investigations in order to support the president’s aim to set tariffs globally and to modify them at any time at the president’s will, and thus strip Congress of the authority to set tariff rates under the taxing power set forth in the Constitution.”

In a separate announcement, the White House also announced a proposed 10 percent tariff on finished aircraft made by Brazilian planemaker Embraer, whose jets are widely used by US regional carriers operating under brands including United Express, Delta Connection and American Eagle. Finished aircraft are Brazil’s fourth-biggest export to the US.

The US also plans to raise duties on imports of Brazilian sugar that exceed quotas as part of an effort to push Brasilia to rectify alleged unfair trade practices, according to a senior US official.

Several governments have reacted to the new tariff announcement, as has the European Union.

“The EU takes note of the publication by the US of preliminary findings pursuant to its Section 301 investigation concerning structural excess capacity in manufacturing sectors,” European Commission spokesperson Olof Gill told Al Jazeera.

“We will study the findings. At the same time we strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity. To the contrary, Europe is among those most exposed to overcapacity,” Gill added.

The Swiss government has also reacted, saying that it rejects the allegations stemming from the investigations.

“The timing right before the G20 [in mid-December] sets up those meetings as an opportunity for negotiation and increases risk of both inflationary pressures and macro volatility in 2027, reducing some of the benefit from easing gas prices,” Rachel Ziemba, adjunct senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security, told Al Jazeera.

“We have been clear throughout the process that Norway does not have policies that contribute to overcapacity. Norwegian companies produce in response to market demand,” Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide said.

US markets are trending down on news of the new tariffs. The tech-heavy Nasdaq tumbled 3.9 percent in early trading on Wednesday. The S&P 500 is down 2.8 percent, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average slumped by 1.4 percent.

The price of gold – which is considered a safe investment in times of economic uncertainty – fell by more than 3 percent to its lowest level in more than a year. However, in addition to tariffs, the price was influenced by inflation data released on Wednesday which showed a 0.3 percent rise in one of the US Federal Reserve’s key metrics for assessing the rate of inflation. Higher inflation increases the chances of a rise in interest rates, which in turn weighs on the metal.

Bond yields in both the US and Europe dropped on Wednesday.

Germany’s 10-year bond yield, which is the benchmark for the eurozone, slid by 4.5 basis points to 3.2 percent, while the US 10-year Treasury note yield stumbled by 6.8 basis points to 4.834 percent, putting it on pace for its seventh daily drop over the past eight sessions.

articles.title: Trump Blames Voters for Stock Market Tanking
articles.summary: It’s never his fault.
articles.body:
President Trump is blaming the voters—not AI anxiety or his own tariffs—on the stock market's poor performance.

"Stocks are down sharply because of the November Third Election results," Trump wrote Wednesday on Truth Social. "I wasn't on the Ballot, but if I was, the results, just like all three times before, would have been much different, and the Stock Market, and your 401-k's, would be BOOMING. I told you so!!!"'

On Wednesday, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell before moderately recovering, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq each dropped . These movements have little to do with the midterm elections—in which Trump's agenda was indeed on the ballot—and more to do with the tariffs he's placing on the European Union, China, Mexico, Japan, South Korea, and 27 other EU members—a policy that has already proven to be economically disastrous . It's one of the major reasons why his party lost the midterms. Now he's doing it again, and blaming it on the very people whom his policy hurt.

articles.title: How the Trump administration determined Jensen Huang is not a national security threat
articles.summary: By Dan Rosenzweig-Ziff, Erin Banco, Jonathan Landay and Andrew Goudsward WASHINGTON, Nov 25 (Reuters) - The US Justice Department did not conduct a formal in...
articles.body:
By Dan Rosenzweig-Ziff, Erin Banco, Jonathan Landay and Andrew Goudsward

WASHINGTON, Nov 25 (Reuters) - The US Justice Department did not conduct a formal investigation into Jensen Huang before US President Donald Trump pushed for his return as Nvidia chief executive this week, despite active probes into the chipmaker's customers and allegations he conducted an affair with a woman linked to Chinese intelligence, according to three people familiar ‌with the matter.

Instead, Attorney General Todd Blanche concluded that there was no evidence the tech titan had broken any laws based on the Justice Department's ongoing investigations into two Nvidia clients, Super Micro Computer and ‌Megaspeed International, which are suspected of smuggling advanced microchips to China, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity.

That determination, which is subject to change as the probes continue, was crucial to Blanche's decision to tell Trump and Vice President JD Vance over the weekend that he possessed ​no evidence that Huang posed a risk to national security, said two of the people.

Jensen Huang's reinstatement has angered members of Congress — both Republicans and Democrats — who say it's too soon to set aside questions about whether Nvidia or its CEO endangered US national security. The lack of any additional effort to examine their roles prior to Trump's intervention will likely fuel a push for more investigations on Capitol Hill.

The Justice Department probes of Nvidia customers found no evidence that Huang was acting as an agent of China or knowingly transferred sensitive semiconductor technology or information to China, the two people said. Nvidia was not a target of those investigations and cooperated, providing documents, interviews and other data that ‌helped lead to that conclusion, they added.

There was also no counterintelligence probe of Huang ⁠himself. US spy agencies have gathered information on Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive and alleged paramour of Jensen Huang suspected of working with Chinese intelligence, said two other people familiar with the effort. But the US had no details that would warrant a probe into the Nvidia CEO, they said.

Counterintelligence investigations are run separately from criminal investigations and are ⁠aimed at monitoring and neutralizing national security threats, rather than building a case for indictment.

Justice Department officials concluded that Nvidia and Huang had committed no wrongdoing and did not suspect its chief executive posed a national-security risk, two of the people familiar with the matter said.

articles.title: How retail investors are flipping the 'balance of power' in markets
articles.summary: Retail investors are having a larger impact than ever on markets, according to stock market veteran Barbara Doran, CEO of BD8 Capital Partners.
articles.body:
Retail investors are having a larger impact than ever on markets, according to one stock market veteran.

The "balance of power has really changed" in markets as the number of everyday Americans trading stocks has grown, BD8 Capital Partners CEO Barbara Doran told Yahoo Finance on The 8:30 . She noted that market size has increased, reducing the power of institutional heavyweights.

The volatility in individual stocks often "has nothing to do with fundamentals," Doran said, pointing to the rise in algorithmic and momentum trading among retail investors and hedge funds repositioning. Meanwhile, she added, some institutional investors that previously could have been those "steady hands" are staying on the sidelines.

"You saw what happened last year, how many times this 'buy on weakness' … was retail that was saving the markets," Doran said. "You know, when the institutions were holding back to wait to see, retail's like, 'Ooh, buying opportunity.'"

Anthropic ( ANT ) is one name with a big retail presence, as its public debut set a record for retail trading activity with $772 million in shares traded on its first day. But the share of buyers was less than anticipated, according to Vanda Research.

While discussing Anthropic's recent slide below the Claude maker's IPO price of $83, Doran said a number of factors are likely driving a range of investors to consider selling or at least hesitate before buying the stock.

"As underwriters, they try to put a stock in what they call steady hands, you know, big institutions that are not going to sell it," Doran said. "But, you know, if you didn't get enough stock or you have a huge pop-up … you go, 'Hmm, it would be stupid to not take the money off the table.'"

Still, some investors have stepped in amid the stock's weakness. Anthropic stock climbed back above the $85 mark in Wednesday trading, bucking the trend of a broadly negative day for tech stocks , with the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) down as much as 2% before paring back losses this afternoon.

articles.title: SpaceX, Elon Musk to give one share each to active Trump Accounts
articles.summary: SpaceX and Elon Musk promise to donate one share each to active Trump accounts.
articles.body:
SpaceX ( SPCX ) said Wednesday it will give one share of its Class A stock to every active Trump Account, with CEO Elon Musk personally matching the company's contribution.

"SpaceX is building the infrastructure of the future and working to make life multiplanetary," the company said in a statement . "We believe ownership of the company creating these systems should extend to the next generation of Americans for their long-term benefit."

SpaceX also said president and COO Gwynne Shotwell had separately announced a personal gift of more than 2 million shares.

Trump Accounts are tax-advantaged investment accounts for children, created under the president's 2025 tax law. The program officially launched in July, with the government providing a one-time $1,000 contribution for eligible children born from 2025 through 2028.

Last month, the White House said nearly 70 million Trump Accounts had been created, including more than 60 million through automatic enrollment.

Since the July 4 launch, more than $4.5 billion has been deposited, including $1.3 billion in $1,000 government seed contributions, according to the White House.

Other public companies have also pledged funds to the accounts. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a CNBC interview last week that an Anthropic ( ANT ) co-founder will make a "large gift" to Trump Accounts in the coming weeks.

"We believe that it's important for these great entrepreneurs to share their bounty," he added.
